claim: Pcm1−/− mice were present at normal Mendelian ratios at late gestation (embryonic day [E] 18.5)
source: Pcm1−/− mice were present at normal Mendelian ratios at late gestation (embryonic day [E] 18.5) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing genotyping results at E18.5.

claim: By postnatal day (P) 5, half of Pcm1−/− mice had died
source: However, by postnatal day (P) 5, half of Pcm1−/− mice had died (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), revealing that PCM1 is important for perinatal survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PCM1 is important for perinatal survival
source: However, by postnatal day (P) 5, half of Pcm1−/− mice had died (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), revealing that PCM1 is important for perinatal survival.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that half of Pcm1−/− mice died by P5.

claim: Surviving Pcm1−/− mice were smaller than littermate controls, weighing less than half of controls at P28
source: Surviving Pcm1−/− mice were smaller than littermate controls, weighing less than half of controls at P28 (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: Dwarfism in Pcm1−/− mice was detectable before birth, indicating intrauterine growth retardation
source: This dwarfism was detectable before birth, indicating intrauterine growth retardation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by embryo weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The brains of surviving Pcm1−/− mice were proportionally smaller than those of littermates
source: The brains of surviving Pcm1−/− mice were proportionally smaller than those of littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G), and displayed marked hydrocephaly (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by brain weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Pcm1−/− mice displayed marked hydrocephaly
source: The brains of surviving Pcm1−/− mice were proportionally smaller than those of littermates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G), and displayed marked hydrocephaly (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by brain imaging and histology shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Hydrocephaly can result from motile cilia dysfunction
source: Hydrocephaly can result from motile cilia dysfunction, raising the possibility that centriolar satellites are required for cilia formation and/or function in ependymal cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between motile cilia dysfunction and hydrocephaly.

claim: Cilia are essential for key events in mammalian development
source: Cilia are essential for key events in mammalian development; mice lacking cilia die during embryogenesis with developmental defects including randomized left–right axes and polydactyly (Ferrante et al., 2006; Huangfu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ferrante et al., 2006; Huangfu et al., 2003).

claim: Many E18.5 Pcm1−/− tissues possessed cilia
source: Many E18.5 Pcm1−/− tissues possessed cilia and Pcm1−/− mice survived at Mendelian ratios to birth and displayed no evidence of situs abnormalities or polydactyly, revealing that centriolar satellites are not required for mammalian ciliogenesis in many cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of cilia in various tissues at E18.5.

claim: Pcm1−/− mice survived at Mendelian ratios to birth and displayed no evidence of situs abnormalities or polydactyly
source: Many E18.5 Pcm1−/− tissues possessed cilia and Pcm1−/− mice survived at Mendelian ratios to birth and displayed no evidence of situs abnormalities or polydactyly, revealing that centriolar satellites are not required for mammalian ciliogenesis in many cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of survival rates and phenotypic analysis of Pcm1−/− mice.

claim: Centriolar satellites are not required for mammalian ciliogenesis in many cell types
source: Many E18.5 Pcm1−/− tissues possessed cilia and Pcm1−/− mice survived at Mendelian ratios to birth and displayed no evidence of situs abnormalities or polydactyly, revealing that centriolar satellites are not required for mammalian ciliogenesis in many cell types.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Pcm1−/− mice have cilia in many tissues and survive to birth without major developmental defects.

claim: Most Pcm1−/− mice died perinatally with hydrocephaly, delayed formation and disrupted function of ependymal cilia, oligospermia, and abnormalities in tracheal epithelial cell ciliogenesis
source: Despite PCM1 being dispensable for ciliogenesis in many tissues, most Pcm1−/− mice died perinatally with hydrocephaly, delayed formation and disrupted function of ependymal cilia, oligospermia, and abnormalities in tracheal epithelial cell ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple observations throughout the manuscript including survival data, histology, and functional assays.

claim: Pcm1−/− mice exhibited cerebellar hypoplasia
source: In addition, Pcm1−/− mice exhibited cerebellar hypoplasia and partially penetrant hydronephrosis, both of which can be caused by defective Hedgehog signaling, a signal transduction pathway dependent on cilia (Huangfu et al., 2003; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of cerebellar size in Pcm1−/− mice.

claim: Pcm1−/− mice exhibited partially penetrant hydronephrosis
source: In addition, Pcm1−/− mice exhibited cerebellar hypoplasia and partially penetrant hydronephrosis, both of which can be caused by defective Hedgehog signaling, a signal transduction pathway dependent on cilia (Huangfu et al., 2003; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cerebellar hypoplasia and hydronephrosis can be caused by defective Hedgehog signaling
source: In addition, Pcm1−/− mice exhibited cerebellar hypoplasia and partially penetrant hydronephrosis, both of which can be caused by defective Hedgehog signaling, a signal transduction pathway dependent on cilia (Huangfu et al., 2003; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Huangfu et al., 2003; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Yu et al., 2002).

claim: Hedgehog signaling is a signal transduction pathway dependent on cilia
source: In addition, Pcm1−/− mice exhibited cerebellar hypoplasia and partially penetrant hydronephrosis, both of which can be caused by defective Hedgehog signaling, a signal transduction pathway dependent on cilia (Huangfu et al., 2003; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PCM1 promotes ciliogenesis in select cell types, many of which possess motile cilia
source: These phenotypes indicate that PCM1 promotes ciliogenesis in select cell types, many of which possess motile cilia.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Pcm1−/− mice have defects in specific ciliated cell types.

claim: Pcm1−/− mice exhibited fewer ependymal cells with multiple basal bodies at P3 and P5
source: Pcm1−/− mice exhibited numerous ependymal cell abnormalities, including fewer ependymal cells with multiple basal bodies at P3 and P5 (Figure 3A-C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of basal bodies in ependymal cells shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By P16, Pcm1−/− mice had caught up and displayed normal numbers of ependymal cells with multiple basal bodies
source: However, by P16, Pcm1−/− mice had caught up and displayed normal numbers of ependymal cells with multiple basal bodies (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of basal bodies in ependymal cells at P16 shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absence of PCM1 causes a delay in centriole biogenesis
source: These results suggest a delay in centriole biogenesis in the absence of PCM1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of delayed basal body formation in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells.

claim: Basal bodies of Pcm1−/− ependymal cells displayed disrupted translational polarity of basal bodies within the apical domain, which persisted until P16
source: In addition, basal bodies of Pcm1−/− ependymal cells displayed disrupted translational polarity of basal bodies within the apical domain, which persisted until P16 (Figure 3B, G, H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by polarity analysis shown in Figure 3B, G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Basal body positioning within the apical domain is thought to be independent of ciliary motility
source: Basal body positioning within the apical domain is thought to be independent of ciliary motility, suggesting roles for PCM1 in ependymal cells beyond motility (Kishimoto and Sawamoto, 2012; Mirzadeh et al., 2010b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kishimoto and Sawamoto, 2012; Mirzadeh et al., 2010b).

claim: Pcm1−/− ependymal cells contained highly elongated FOP- and Centrin-containing centriole-like structures measuring 5.0 ± 1.9 µm in length
source: Interestingly, Pcm1−/− ependymal cells contained highly elongated FOP- and Centrin-containing centriole-like structures measuring 5.0 ± 1.9 µm (mean ± standard deviation [SD]) in length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: At P5, there were fewer Pcm1−/− ciliated ependymal cells
source: At P5, there were fewer Pcm1−/− ciliated ependymal cells. However, by P16, the number of ciliated Pcm1−/− ependymal cells was equivalent to control ventricles (Figure 3A, B, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ciliated cells shown in Figure 3A, B, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: By P16, the number of ciliated Pcm1−/− ependymal cells was equivalent to control ventricles
source: At P5, there were fewer Pcm1−/− ciliated ependymal cells. However, by P16, the number of ciliated Pcm1−/− ependymal cells was equivalent to control ventricles (Figure 3A, B, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ciliated cells shown in Figure 3A, B, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At P3, Pcm1−/− ependymal cilia displayed ultrastructural defects, including missing microtubule doublets and fused axonemes
source: At P3, Pcm1−/− ependymal cilia displayed ultrastructural defects, including missing microtubule doublets and fused axonemes (Figure 3I, K).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3I, K.

claim: Pcm1−/− ependymal cells possessed fewer centrioles at the disengagement stage of centriole biogenesis
source: These Pcm1−/− ependymal cells possessed fewer centrioles at the disengagement stage of centriole biogenesis, but once the cells became multiciliated had normal numbers of centrioles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of centrioles in cultured ependymal cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, G.

claim: Once Pcm1−/− ependymal cells became multiciliated they had normal numbers of centrioles
source: These Pcm1−/− ependymal cells possessed fewer centrioles at the disengagement stage of centriole biogenesis, but once the cells became multiciliated had normal numbers of centrioles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of centrioles in cultured ependymal cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, G.

claim: Pcm1−/− ependymal cells formed fewer cilia than control ependymal cells in culture
source: In culture, Pcm1−/− ependymal cells formed fewer cilia than control ependymal cells (Figure 3J, L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cilia in cultured ependymal cells shown in Figure 3J, L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, F.

claim: Pcm1−/− ependymal cilia beat slowly and uncoordinatedly
source: High-speed video microscopy revealed that Pcm1−/− ependymal cilia beat slowly and uncoordinatedly (Figure 3J, M, N, Figure 3—videos 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-speed video microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3J, M, N and Figure 3—videos 1–3.

claim: PCM1 is not essential for ciliogenesis, but is required for timely basal body biogenesis, maturation, migration, and ciliogenesis in ependymal cells
source: Thus, PCM1 is not essential for ciliogenesis, but is required for timely basal body biogenesis, maturation, migration, and ciliogenesis in ependymal cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations of delayed but eventual ciliogenesis in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells.

claim: Hydrocephaly in Pcm1−/− mice is caused by delayed ependymal cell ciliogenesis and compromised ciliary motility
source: We propose that hydrocephaly in Pcm1−/− mice is caused by delayed ependymal cell ciliogenesis and compromised ciliary motility.
evidence: The claim is a proposed explanation based on observations of ependymal cell defects and hydrocephaly in Pcm1−/− mice.

claim: Pcm1−/− tracheal multiciliated cells in vivo did not display decreased numbers of basal bodies or cilia at P5
source: Pcm1−/− tracheal multiciliated cells in vivo did not display decreased numbers of basal bodies or cilia at P5, or altered axonemal ultrastructure at 6 months of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: Pcm1−/− tracheal cilia beat at normal frequency
source: High-speed video microscopy revealed Pcm1−/− tracheal cilia beat at normal frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E, Figure 3—videos 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-speed video microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and Figure 3—videos 4 and 5.

claim: Pcm1−/− mTECs displayed normal basal body biogenesis, ciliogenesis, and ciliary beat frequency
source: Concurring with a previous reports on the dispensability of PCM1 in mTECs (Vladar and Stearns, 2007), Pcm1−/− mTECs displayed normal basal body biogenesis, ciliogenesis, and ciliary beat frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mTECs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, F and is consistent with previous reports (Vladar and Stearns, 2007).

claim: Many motile ciliary proteins, including dynein motors, dynein assembly factors and dynein docking factors, were reduced early in ciliogenensis (air–liquid interface [ALI] day 7) in Pcm1−/− mTECs
source: However, proteomic analysis of differentiating Pcm1−/− mTECs revealed that many motile ciliary proteins, including dynein motors, dynein assembly factors and dynein docking factors, were reduced early in ciliogenensis (air–liquid interface [ALI] day 7) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Proteomic differences in Pcm1−/− mTECs resolved by ALI day 21
source: Similar to the transitory delay we observed in Pcm1−/− ependymal cell ciliogenesis, proteomic differences in Pcm1−/− mTECs resolved by ALI day 21 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and Supplementary file 5.

claim: PCM1 promotes timely cilia maturation in tracheal cells
source: Thus, as in ependymal cells, PCM1 promotes timely cilia maturation in tracheal cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of transient proteomic differences in Pcm1−/− mTECs.

claim: In multiciliated cells, PCM1 and other centriolar satellite proteins including CEP131 and PCNT localize to fibrogranular material, satellite-like networks
source: In multiciliated cells, PCM1 and other centriolar satellite proteins including CEP131 and PCNT localize to fibrogranular material, satellite-like networks (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Zhao et al., 2021).

claim: CEP131 in mTECs lacking PCM1 localized not to fibrogranular material but to centrioles
source: Consistent with previous findings from Zhao et al., we found that CEP131 in mTECs lacking PCM1 localized not to fibrogranular material but to centrioles, (Figure 3O).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3O and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: In Pcm1−/− ependymal cells, CEP131 mislocalized to the centrioles, although rather than being absent from the fibrogranular material, this non-centriolar CEP131 pool became more elongated
source: Similarly, in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells, CEP131 mislocalized to the centrioles, although rather than being absent from the fibrogranular material, this non-centriolar CEP131 pool became more elongated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Localization of PCNT was normal in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells
source: Not all centriolar satellite components behaved similarly in the absence of PCM1; localization of PCNT was normal in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Fibrogranular material in the absence of PCM1 can either be disrupted or change its distribution in different multiciliated cell types
source: Thus, fibrogranular material in the absence of PCM1 can either be disrupted or change its distribution in different multiciliated cell types.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of different effects on fibrogranular material in different cell types lacking PCM1.

claim: PCM1 is required for fibrogranular material integrity, centriole biogenesis, and migration, and timely ciliogenesis in multiciliated cells
source: Together, these results suggest that PCM1 is required for fibrogranular material integrity, centriole biogenesis, and migration, and timely ciliogenesis in multiciliated cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations of defects in Pcm1−/− multiciliated cells.

claim: In control RPE1 cells, CEP131 and CEP290 localized to both centriolar satellites and to the centrioles themselves
source: In control RPE1 cells, CEP131 and CEP290 localized to both centriolar satellites and to the centrioles themselves.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations in control RPE1 cells.

claim: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, the centriolar satellite pool of CEP131 was absent, CEP290 was reduced and dispersed, and both displayed increased accumulation at centrioles
source: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, the centriolar satellite pool of CEP131 was absent, CEP290 was reduced and dispersed, and both displayed increased accumulation at centrioles (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: In control MEFs, CEP131 and MIB1 localized to both centriolar satellites and to the centrioles themselves
source: In control MEFs, CEP131 and MIB1 localized to both centriolar satellites and to the centrioles themselves.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence observations in control MEFs.

claim: In Pcm1−/− MEFs, the centriolar satellite pool of CEP131 was absent and MIB1 was reduced and dispersed, with CEP131 displaying increased accumulation at centrioles
source: In Pcm1−/− MEFs, the centriolar satellite pool of CEP131 was absent and MIB1 was reduced and dispersed, with CEP131 displaying increased accumulation at centrioles, similar to Pcm1−/− tracheal epithelial cells (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4D–G.

claim: PCM1 is critical for centriolar satellite integrity
source: We conclude that PCM1 is critical for centriolar satellite integrity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of disrupted satellite localization of multiple proteins in the absence of PCM1.

claim: In the absence of satellites, some satellite proteins (e.g., CEP131 and CEP290) over-accumulate at centrioles, while others (e.g., MIB1) do not
source: In the absence of satellites, some satellite proteins (e.g., CEP131 and CEP290) over-accumulate at centrioles, while others (e.g., MIB1) do not, highlighting the protein-specific role centriolar satellites play in controlling centriolar localization.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of differential effects on different satellite proteins in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: Centriolar satellites both deliver and remove select cargos from centrioles
source: We propose that centriolar satellites both deliver and remove select cargos from centrioles.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on observations of protein localization changes in the absence of PCM1.

claim: Ciliogenesis was abrogated in several PCM1−/− RPE1 cell lines
source: In accordance with previous observations (Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016), ciliogenesis was abrogated in several PCM1−/− RPE1 cell lines (Figure 4H, J) and could be rescued by expression of eYFP-PCM1 (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of ciliated cells shown in Figure 4H, J and is consistent with previous observations (Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Abrogated ciliogenesis in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells could be rescued by expression of eYFP-PCM1
source: In accordance with previous observations (Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016), ciliogenesis was abrogated in several PCM1−/− RPE1 cell lines (Figure 4H, J) and could be rescued by expression of eYFP-PCM1 (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Ciliogenesis was not perturbed in Pcm1−/− MEFs
source: In marked contrast, and consistent with the tissue-specific effects of loss of PCM1 on ciliogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), ciliogenesis was not perturbed in Pcm1−/− MEFs, with Pcm1−/− MEFs displaying cilia number, centrosome number and cilia length indistinguishable from those of controls (Figure 4K, M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cilia in MEFs shown in Figure 4K, M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: PCM1 plays cell-type-specific roles in ciliogenesis
source: Thus, PCM1, despite broad roles in regulating the centriolar localization of proteins such as CEP131, plays cell-type-specific roles in ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of differential effects of PCM1 loss on ciliogenesis in different cell types.

claim: Both Talpid3 and Centrobin localization to centrioles in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells was equivalent to those of controls
source: We found that both Talpid3 and Centrobin localization to centrioles in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells was equivalent to those of controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Talpid3 recruitment to centrioles and Centrobin removal from the mother centriole are not dependent upon PCM1 or centriolar satellites
source: Thus, Talpid3 recruitment to centrioles and Centrobin removal from the mother centriole are not dependent upon PCM1 or, by extension, centriolar satellites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that Talpid3 and Centrobin localization are normal in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, both distal and subdistal appendage components localized to the mother centriole
source: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, both distal and subdistal appendage components localized to the mother centriole (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–K), although the amount of distal appendage proteins at the mother centriole was slightly reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–K.

claim: Serial section transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed that subdistal and distal appendages were present in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells
source: Serial section transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed that subdistal and distal appendages were present in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Centriolar satellites are not required for the assembly of distal or subdistal appendages at the mother centriole
source: Therefore, centriolar satellites are not required for the assembly of distal or subdistal appendages at the mother centriole.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that appendages are present in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced Myosin-Va at preciliary vesicles
source: Using 3D-SIM imaging of Myosin-Va, we identified preciliary vesicles at the basal bodies of control RPE1 cells soon after the induction of ciliogenesis (i.e., after 1 hr of serum starvation). PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced Myosin-Va at preciliary vesicles (Figure 5A, B), suggesting that centriolar satellites promote timely centriolar docking of preciliary vesicles.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D-SIM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Centriolar satellites promote timely centriolar docking of preciliary vesicles
source: Using 3D-SIM imaging of Myosin-Va, we identified preciliary vesicles at the basal bodies of control RPE1 cells soon after the induction of ciliogenesis (i.e., after 1 hr of serum starvation). PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced Myosin-Va at preciliary vesicles (Figure 5A, B), suggesting that centriolar satellites promote timely centriolar docking of preciliary vesicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of reduced Myosin-Va at preciliary vesicles in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced RAB34 at both centrosomes and ciliary sheaths
source: PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced RAB34 at both centrosomes and ciliary sheaths (Figure 5C, D), suggesting that centriolar satellites promote timely docking of the mother centriole to the preciliary vesicles, and the fusion of preciliary vesicles into a ciliary vesicle.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D-SIM imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: Centriolar satellites promote timely docking of the mother centriole to the preciliary vesicles, and the fusion of preciliary vesicles into a ciliary vesicle
source: PCM1−/− RPE1 cells showed reduced RAB34 at both centrosomes and ciliary sheaths (Figure 5C, D), suggesting that centriolar satellites promote timely docking of the mother centriole to the preciliary vesicles, and the fusion of preciliary vesicles into a ciliary vesicle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of reduced RAB34 at centrosomes and ciliary sheaths in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: In PCM1−/− cells, mother centrioles exhibited reduced association with preciliary and ciliary vesicles
source: In PCM1−/− cells, mother centrioles (identified by the presence of distal and subdistal appendages) exhibited reduced association with preciliary and ciliary vesicles (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section TEM analysis shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Centriolar satellites promote the attachment of the mother centriole to preciliary vesicles and formation of the ciliary vesicle
source: Thus, centriolar satellites promote the attachment of the mother centriole to preciliary vesicles and formation of the ciliary vesicle, important early steps in ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations of reduced vesicle association in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: CP110 and CEP97 persisted at the distal mother centriole in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells after 24 hr of serum starvation
source: In contrast to control cells, CP110 and CEP97 persisted at the distal mother centriole in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells after 24 hr of serum starvation (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6A–D.

claim: In wild-type MEFs, a small amount of CP110 persisted on the mother centriole even after axoneme formation
source: Interestingly, in wild-type MEFs, a small amount of CP110 persisted on the mother centriole even after axoneme formation (Figure 6E, G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6E, G, H.

claim: Mother centrioles in Pcm1−/− MEFs had CP110 levels comparable to daughter centrioles after 24 hr serum starvation, despite undergoing ciliogenesis at rates equal to that of wild-type cells
source: Strikingly, mother centrioles in Pcm1−/− MEFs had CP110 levels comparable to daughter centrioles after 24 hr serum starvation, despite undergoing ciliogenesis at rates equal to that of wild-type cells (Figure 6E, G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6E, G, H.

claim: PCM1 is essential for removing CP110 from the mother centriole, but CP110 removal is not required for ciliogenesis in MEFs
source: Thus, PCM1 is essential for removing CP110 from the mother centriole, but CP110 removal is not required for ciliogenesis in MEFs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that Pcm1−/− MEFs retain CP110 but still form cilia.

claim: In Pcm1−/− ependymal cells in vivo, CP110 levels were elevated at P3
source: Similar to RPE1 cells and MEFs, in Pcm1−/− ependymal cells in vivo, CP110 levels were elevated at P3, an age when ependymal calls are engaged in ciliogenesis (Figure 6F, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6F, I.

claim: CP110 levels were elevated at the multiple basal bodies of Pcm1−/− tracheal multiciliated cells
source: Moreover, CP110 levels were elevated at the multiple basal bodies of Pcm1−/− tracheal multiciliated cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diverse cell types require PCM1 to remove CP110 from the mother centriole, despite differentially requiring PCM1 for ciliogenesis
source: Thus, diverse cell types require PCM1 to remove CP110 from the mother centriole, despite differentially requiring PCM1 for ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of elevated CP110 in multiple Pcm1−/− cell types with different ciliogenesis outcomes.

claim: Localization of both IFT88 and IFT81 at mother centrioles was reduced in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells
source: Localization of both IFT88 and IFT81 at mother centrioles was reduced in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells (Figure 7A–D), suggesting that IFT recruitment to the mother centriole is promoted by centriolar satellites.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: IFT recruitment to the mother centriole is promoted by centriolar satellites
source: Localization of both IFT88 and IFT81 at mother centrioles was reduced in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells (Figure 7A–D), suggesting that IFT recruitment to the mother centriole is promoted by centriolar satellites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of reduced IFT localization in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: Ciliary and basal body levels of IFT88 were normal in Pcm1−/− MEFs
source: In contrast, ciliary and basal body levels of IFT88 were normal in Pcm1−/− MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating a concordance between PCM1-dependent IFT recruitment and ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: There is a concordance between PCM1-dependent IFT recruitment and ciliogenesis
source: In contrast, ciliary and basal body levels of IFT88 were normal in Pcm1−/− MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating a concordance between PCM1-dependent IFT recruitment and ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that IFT recruitment is affected in cell types where ciliogenesis is affected, but not in MEFs where ciliogenesis is normal.

claim: Recruitment of CEP162 to the mother centriole was unaffected in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells
source: Recruitment of CEP162 to the mother centriole was unaffected in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7E, F.

claim: PCM1−/− RPE1 cells exhibited reduced RPGRIP1L at the transition zone
source: In contrast, PCM1−/− RPE1 cells exhibited reduced RPGRIP1L at the transition zone (Figure 7G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7G, H.

claim: Centriolar satellites promote both IFT recruitment and transition zone formation at RPE1 cell mother centrioles
source: Therefore, centriolar satellites promote both IFT recruitment and transition zone formation at RPE1 cell mother centrioles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of reduced IFT and transition zone components in PCM1−/− RPE1 cells.

claim: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, TTBK2 recruitment to distal mother centrioles was equivalent to that of control cells
source: In PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, TTBK2 recruitment to distal mother centrioles was equivalent to that of control cells (Figure 7I, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7I, J.

claim: Centriolar satellites regulate CP110 and CEP97 removal from the distal mother centriole through a mechanism independent of TTBK2 recruitment
source: These results suggest that centriolar satellites regulate CP110 and CEP97 removal from the distal mother centriole through a mechanism independent of TTBK2 recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that TTBK2 recruitment is normal but CP110/CEP97 removal is impaired in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: CP110 and CEP97 colocalized with PCM1 and CEP290 at centriolar satellites in cycling cells
source: We examined RPE1 cells for CP110 and CEP97 and found that, indeed, CP110 and CEP97 colocalized with PCM1 and CEP290 at centriolar satellites in cycling cells (Figure 8A, B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8A, B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, C.

claim: The satellite pool of CP110 was absent in PCM1−/− RPE cells
source: Moreover, this satellite pool of CP110 was absent in PCM1−/− RPE cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CP110 and CEP97 co-immunoprecipitated with PCM1 in cycling cells
source: Consistent with CP110 and CEP97 co-localizing with PCM1 at centriolar satellites, CP110 and CEP97 co-immunoprecipitated with PCM1 in cycling cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The localization of CP110 and CEP97 to centrioles and centriolar satellites was dynamic during ciliogenesis
source: By examining RPE1 cells at different timepoints after serum depletion, we observed that the localization of CP110 and CEP97 to centrioles and centriolar satellites was dynamic: 1 hr after initiating ciliogenesis, CP110 and CEP97 at satellites decreased and, by 24 hr of serum depletion, CP110 and CEP97 were absent from the mother centriole (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: CP110 no longer localized to satellites in cycling RPE1 cells upon CEP290 knockdown
source: Consistent with this model, CP110 no longer localized to satellites in cycling RPE1 cells upon CEP290 knockdown (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of CEP290 knockdown cells shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CP110 and CEP97 are centriolar satellite cargos which are wicked away from mother centrioles by centriolar satellites during early ciliogenesis
source: We propose that CP110 and CEP97 are centriolar satellite cargos which are wicked away from mother centrioles by centriolar satellites during early ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on observations of CP110/CEP97 localization dynamics and dependence on PCM1 and CEP290.

claim: In serum-starved PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, both CEP290 and CP110 were modestly elevated relative to serum-starved control cells
source: In serum-starved PCM1−/− RPE1 cells, both CEP290 and CP110 were modestly elevated relative to serum-starved control cells (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8D, E.

claim: In synchronized RPE1 cells, CP110 levels were increased in the absence of PCM1, most markedly during mitosis and G0
source: Similarly, in synchronized RPE1 cells, CP110 levels were increased in the absence of PCM1, most markedly during mitosis and G0 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis of synchronized cells shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the absence of PCM1, CP110 and CEP97 over-accumulated at both centrioles
source: Using immunofluorescence microscopy of cycling cells treated with nocodazole, we examined the localization of CP110 and CEP97 to centrioles. In the absence of PCM1, CP110, and CEP97 over-accumulated at both centrioles (Figure 8F–I), suggesting that centriolar satellites restrict CP110 and CEP97 accumulation at centrioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 8F–I.

claim: Centriolar satellites restrict CP110 and CEP97 accumulation at centrioles
source: Using immunofluorescence microscopy of cycling cells treated with nocodazole, we examined the localization of CP110 and CEP97 to centrioles. In the absence of PCM1, CP110, and CEP97 over-accumulated at both centrioles (Figure 8F–I), suggesting that centriolar satellites restrict CP110 and CEP97 accumulation at centrioles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of CP110 and CEP97 over-accumulation at centrioles in PCM1−/− cells.

claim: Centriolar satellites restrict CP110 and CEP97 levels at centrioles, the removal of which promotes ciliogenesis in specific cell types
source: We conclude that centriolar satellites restrict CP110 and CEP97 levels at centrioles, the removal of which promotes ciliogenesis in specific cell types.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on multiple observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Centriolar satellites help promote timely ciliary vesicle formation and remove CP110 and CEP97 from the mother centriole, enabling recruitment of IFT and construction of the transition zone
source: Centriolar satellites help promote timely ciliary vesicle formation and remove CP110 and CEP97 from the mother centriole, enabling recruitment of IFT and construction of the transition zone, early steps in ciliogenesis important for the prevention of ciliopathy-associated phenotypes such as hydrocephaly (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is a summary of multiple findings presented throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: PCM1 is both a component of centriolar satellites and necessary for centriolar satellite formation
source: PCM1 is both a component of centriolar satellites and necessary for centriolar satellite formation (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Kubo and Tsukita, 2003; Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Kubo and Tsukita, 2003; Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: Centriolar satellites are dynamic, change in response to cell stresses, and have been implicated in diverse processes including Hedgehog signaling, autophagy, proteasome activity, and aggresome formation
source: Centriolar satellites are dynamic, change in response to cell stresses, and have been implicated in diverse processes including Hedgehog signaling, autophagy, proteasome activity, and aggresome formation (Holdgaard et al., 2019; Hori and Toda, 2017; Joachim et al., 2017; Kubo and Tsukita, 2003; Lecland and Merdes, 2018; Odabasi et al., 2019; Prosser et al., 2022; Prosser and Pelletier, 2020; Tang et al., 2013; Tollenaere et al., 2015; Villumsen et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Genetic perturbation of centriolar satellite components can compromise cilia formation and contribute to human ciliopathies and microcephaly
source: Possibly reflecting involvement in these diverse biological processes, genetic perturbation of centriolar satellite components can compromise cilia formation and contribute to human ciliopathies and microcephaly (Conkar et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2008; Klinger et al., 2014; Kurtulmus et al., 2016; Lee and Stearns, 2013; Mikule et al., 2007; Staples et al., 2014), perhaps in a cell-type-specific way (Monroe et al., 2020; Odabasi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Abrogation of cilia themselves results in midgestation lethality
source: As abrogation of cilia themselves results in midgestation lethality (Huangfu et al., 2003), the presence of Pcm1−/− embryos late in gestation suggests that PCM1 is not essential for all ciliogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Huangfu et al., 2003).

claim: In the postnatal brain, primary cilia are critical for Hedgehog signaling in cerebellar granule cell precursors
source: In the postnatal brain, primary cilia are critical for Hedgehog signaling in cerebellar granule cell precursors.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Decreased cerebellar Hedgehog signaling attenuates expansion of the granule cell precursors
source: Decreased cerebellar Hedgehog signaling attenuates expansion of the granule cell precursors (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999; Spassky et al., 2008; Wallace, 1999; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999).

claim: Pcm1−/− mice displayed ataxia
source: As the cerebellum is important for motor coordination, we analyzed the gait of surviving Pcm1−/− mice. Consistent with altered cerebellar function, Pcm1−/− mice displayed ataxia (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by gait analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A proportion of viable Pcm1−/− mice (n = 2/15) developed hydronephrosis
source: We investigated whether Pcm1−/− mice exhibit other Hedgehog-associated phenotypes. A proportion of viable Pcm1−/− mice (n = 2/15) developed hydronephrosis (Figure 2H), which can also result from attenuated Hedgehog signaling (Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Hydronephrosis can result from attenuated Hedgehog signaling
source: We investigated whether Pcm1−/− mice exhibit other Hedgehog-associated phenotypes. A proportion of viable Pcm1−/− mice (n = 2/15) developed hydronephrosis (Figure 2H), which can also result from attenuated Hedgehog signaling (Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Yu et al., 2002).

claim: Pcm1−/− mice did not display characteristic features of photoreceptor death
source: Pcm1−/− mice did not display characteristic features of photoreceptor death, such as changes to retinal pigmentation on fundoscopy or reduction of the outer nuclear layer on histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fundal imaging and histology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Electroretinogram (ERG) testing at 9 months of age revealed no visual functional deficits in Pcm1−/− mice
source: Electroretinogram (ERG) testing at 9 months of age revealed no visual functional deficits in Pcm1−/− mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by ERG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: PCM1 is not essential for photoreceptor survival
source: Therefore, PCM1 is not essential for photoreceptor survival, suggesting it is dispensable for photoreceptor ciliogenesis and ciliary trafficking.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that Pcm1−/− mice have normal photoreceptor structure and function.

claim: Surviving Pcm1−/− male mice were infertile with reduced sperm in seminiferous tubules
source: Surviving Pcm1−/− male mice were infertile with reduced sperm in seminiferous tubules (Figure 2I–K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm counts and histology shown in Figure 2I–K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The few Pcm1−/− sperm identified exhibited disrupted head-to-tail coupling, abnormal head morphology indicative of defective intramanchette trafficking, and immotility
source: The few Pcm1−/− sperm identified exhibited disrupted head-to-tail coupling, abnormal head morphology indicative of defective intramanchette trafficking, and immotility (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—videos 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by histology and video microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—videos 1–3.

claim: Centriolar satellites are essential for mammalian spermatogenesis and male fertility
source: We previously discovered similar defects in male mice lacking centriolar satellite component CEP131 (also known as AZI1) (Hall et al., 2013), consistent with the idea that centriolar satellites are essential for mammalian spermatogenesis and male fertility.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations in both Pcm1−/− and Cep131−/− mice, supported by a citation to a previous study (Hall et al., 2013).

claim: During the perinatal period, ependymal cells lining the brain ventricles generate many motile cilia
source: During the perinatal period, ependymal cells lining the brain ventricles generate many motile cilia.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Shortly after birth (P1), immature ependymal cells possess non-polarized, short cilia
source: Shortly after birth (P1), immature ependymal cells possess non-polarized, short cilia.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Beginning at P3, ependymal cells form multiple long, polarized cilia; this ciliogenesis occurs in a wave across the ventricle from caudal to rostral
source: Beginning at P3, ependymal cells form multiple long, polarized cilia; this ciliogenesis occurs in a wave across the ventricle from caudal to rostral.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: By P15, ependymal cilia mature to generate metachronal rhythm
source: By P15, ependymal cilia mature to generate metachronal rhythm (Spassky et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Spassky et al., 2008).

claim: Knockdown of Pcm1 in cultured ependymal cells led to disrupted cilia ultrastructure and motility
source: Recent work showed that knockdown of Pcm1 in cultured ependymal cells led to disrupted cilia ultrastructure and motility (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Zhao et al., 2021).

claim: Centriolar satellites move both toward and away from the ciliary base, with frequent fission and fusion at the ciliary base
source: Consistent with previous reports (Conkar et al., 2019), centriolar satellites moved both toward and away from the ciliary base, with frequent fission and fusion at the ciliary base (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging shown in Figure 4—video 1 and is consistent with previous reports (Conkar et al., 2019).
